analysis.one_liner: Lets mining companies use federal public land for mine waste dumps and tailings without proving the land contains minable minerals.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 219-198 on December 18, 2025, almost entirely along party lines, and it now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal mining law so that mining companies can use public land for waste rock dumps, tailings ponds, and other mine-support facilities even when that land contains no minable minerals. It responds to a 2022 court decision (the Rosemont case) that had blocked a copper mine partly on those grounds. The bill also creates a fund, paid for by fees on the new mining claims, to help clean up abandoned hardrock mines.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies that operate, or want to open, hardrock mines on federal land. After a 2022 court ruling limited their ability to claim land for waste dumps unless that land contained valuable minerals, this bill restores their ability to use public land for waste storage regardless of mineral validity. The abandoned-mine cleanup fund is a modest benefit for reclamation work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hardrock mining companies on public land

how_it_helps.text: It reverses, by statute, the Ninth Circuit's 2022 Rosemont decision, which held that miners could only claim land containing valuable minerals for waste disposal.
Mining operators may locate as many mill site claims as they reasonably need (up to 5 acres each) for waste rock and tailings, and may use public land under an approved plan of operations.
It creates an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund, funded by claim-maintenance fees on the new mill sites, to pay for cleanup of abandoned hardrock mines.

analysis.who_pays: The public. The land used for waste disposal is federal public land — shared open space, wildlife habitat, and water sources — and the U.S. gets no royalties on hardrock minerals removed from it. Any water or land contamination from tailings and waste rock ultimately falls on surrounding communities and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets mining companies use federal land for waste disposal even where no valuable mineral deposit has been established, reversing a 2022 court decision that had limited that use — expanding industry access to public land.

Hardrock mining on federal land operates under the 1872 Mining Law without paying royalties on the minerals it removes; this bill expands operators' rights without imposing royalty or stronger cleanup liability terms.

The Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund is funded only by claim-maintenance fees on the new mill sites, so cleanup money depends on how many claims operators actually stake — it is not a guaranteed large revenue stream.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's upside is real but modest: legal clarity after the Rosemont ruling and a dedicated abandoned-mine cleanup fund paid from claim fees. The cost is broader: mining companies gain expanded access to public land for waste disposal without having to show any mineral deposit is worth mining, and the industry continues to extract hardrock minerals from federal land without paying royalties on them — a subsidy ordinary taxpayers effectively finance. The cleanup fund, while helpful, is small relative to the scale of abandoned mine pollution.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 219-198 in December 2025, nearly all Republicans in favor, and the bill has been sitting on the Senate calendar since March 2026 with no vote taken.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on September 17, 2025, by a 25-17 vote, and reported it amended on November 25, 2025.
On December 18, 2025, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit the bill 205-213, with all 205 voting Democrats in favor and every voting Republican against.
The House then passed the bill 219-198, with 210 of 220 voting Republicans in favor and only 9 of 213 voting Democrats.
The Senate received the bill in December 2025 and placed it on its legislative calendar on March 17, 2026; no Senate vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hardrock mining companies — the bill passed the House and now awaits Senate action, with no final law yet either way.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost entirely along party lines: 210 of 220 voting Republicans backed final passage while only 9 of 213 voting Democrats did, and every voting Democrat supported the motion to recommit against unified Republican opposition.

industries.note: The bill overturns the Rosemont decision's limits and lets operators use public land for waste dumps and tailings regardless of mineral validity, at low statutory cost. It locks in the industry's access to federal land under the 1872 Mining Law.
Abandoned hardrock mine reclamation funded by the new fee-fed fund creates paid cleanup work.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is on the Senate calendar but has not been scheduled for a vote; with unified Democratic opposition in the House and the 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation in a closely divided Senate, its odds of becoming law this Congress are low, though it could be attached to a larger package.
